title: Bay du Nord offshore oil project off N.L. clears last major regulatory hurdle
summary: Whether or not the Bay du Nord offshore oil project moves ahead is now up to the companies behind it, as the project has secured its last milestone approval from government.

image.caption: If it goes ahead, Bay du Nord off the coast of Newfoundland will be Canada's first deepwater oil development. (Equinor Canada)

blocks.text: Whether or not the Bay du Nord offshore oil project moves ahead is now up to the companies behind it, as the project has secured its last milestone approval from government.
Ministers approve development after recommendation from Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Energy Regulator

The governments of Canada and Newfoundland and Labrador have signed off on the development application of lead proponent Equinor for the development in the Flemish Pass Basin, about 500 kilometres east of St. John's.
There are other regulatory pieces and permits required, but the development application is considered the last regulatory milestone for the oil project.
“It is a key step in turning this project into real economic opportunities for our people,” said Premier Tony Wakeham at a news conference on Friday afternoon.
The Bay du Nord project has a capital cost estimate of roughly $14 billion.

blocks.text: Wakeham was joined by provincial Energy Minister Lloyd Parrott and federal cabinet minister Joanne Thompson, who is also the MP for St. John's East.
The expectation is the project will generate at least $20 billion in government revenues, while contributing about $50 billion to the country's GDP.

The project has faced strong headwinds, with opposition focused on its distance from shore, its status as the first deep water oil project for Canada and the greenhouse gas emissions to be generated from the use of petroleum products to be created from crude oil produced.

Former federal Environment and Climate Change minister Steven Guilbeault, a climate activist prior to entering the House of Commons, has spoken openly since leaving office about his approval of clearance from environmental impact assessment being one of his most difficult days as minister.
The project met all requirements and cleared impact assessment in April 2022. The decision has withstood court challenge.

blocks.text: The development application is a separate review process, completed by the joint Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator, with agency approval and a recommendation for approval put to the governments on Nov. 4.

The province of Newfoundland and Labrador is poised to become a direct investor in the offshore oil project, signaling earlier this month its intention to take a 10 per cent equity stake, to become a partner alongside Equinor and minority partner Shell.
That will become a firm commitment if the numbers work out, Wakeham has said, with a detailed review in progress.
Should the proponents opt to move the project forward, the province will have up to 90 days after that decision to settle its stake.
A final investment decision is expected in the first quarter of 2027.
